\section[el preso]{el preso — the prisoner}

\label{lesson:ES-C523-preso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to sentence, then the Spanish for the prison.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el preso}
\textbf{el preso} — \textquotedblleft{}the prisoner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El preso salió de la cárcel ayer.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The prisoner came out of prison yesterday.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la presa}. As an adjective: \emph{Está preso} — he is in prison.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{preso} is inherited from Latin \emph{prēnsus}, a shorter form of \emph{prehēnsus} 'seized' (EtymDB), the participle of \emph{prehendere} 'to take hold of'. A prisoner is a person who has been seized.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el preso}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el preso}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el preso}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to sentence, then the Spanish for the prison, then say \emph{el preso} again
\end{itemize}

\section[acusar]{acusar — to accuse}

\label{lesson:ES-C523-acusar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the prison, then the Spanish for the prisoner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acusar}
\textbf{acusar} — \textquotedblleft{}to accuse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Lo acusaron de robar el dinero.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They accused him of stealing the money.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Acusar a alguien de algo} — to accuse someone of something.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acusar} comes from Latin \emph{accūsāre} 'to call to account' (EtymDB), built on \emph{ad} and \emph{causa} 'a case at law'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[confesar]{confesar — to confess}

\label{lesson:ES-C523-confesar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the prisoner, then the Spanish for to accuse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: confesar}
\textbf{confesar} — \textquotedblleft{}to confess\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Al final confesó la verdad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In the end he confessed the truth.}
\end{quote}

Stem change: \emph{confieso}, \emph{confiesas}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{confesar} is usually traced to a spoken Latin verb made from \emph{cōnfessus}, the participle of \emph{cōnfitērī} 'to acknowledge, to confess' (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{fatērī} 'to admit'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[testificar]{testificar — to testify}

\label{lesson:ES-C523-testificar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to accuse, then the Spanish for to confess.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: testificar}
\textbf{testificar} — \textquotedblleft{}to testify\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La vecina testificó en el juicio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The neighbour testified at the trial.}
\end{quote}

It takes \emph{qu} before \emph{e}: \emph{testifiqué}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{testificar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{testificārī} 'to bear witness' (EtymDB), built on \emph{testis} 'a witness' and \emph{facere} 'to make'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[liberar]{liberar — to free, to release}

\label{lesson:ES-C523-liberar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to confess, then the Spanish for to testify.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: liberar}
\textbf{liberar} — \textquotedblleft{}to free, to release\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Liberaron a los presos el lunes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The prisoners were released on Monday.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Liberar a alguien} — to set someone free.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{liberar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{līberāre} 'to set free' (EtymDB), built on \emph{līber} 'free'. It is not the \emph{liber} 'bark, book' behind \emph{libro}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
